source: Langley (1977) BACON: A production system that discovers empirical laws (IJCAI-77)
finding: First BACON. Task world is an artificial 2D universe with labelled objects. A small set of OPS production rules acts as parallel regularity detectors over attribute-object-time-value tuples. A constancy triggers a generalisation. A trend triggers a new defined attribute (change over time, or a product of two attributes that move in opposite directions). The law is the higher-level attribute that turns out constant.
numbers: Example law: the third differential of each object's distance from the centre is constant (different constant per object). Data collection starts random, then is steered by regularities found. Hypotheses are never rejected, only qualified with exceptions and bounds.
quote: BACON discovers empirical laws by using two complementary techniques
limits: Authors list own limits: no conditional laws, built-in knowledge that time and objects are the dimensions to generalise over, no noise handling. Toy world with programmer-set laws.
agent_relevance: The core move is generate-and-test where the generator is a short list of data-driven rules (constancy, monotone trend, product, ratio). Maps to a small operator library fired by signals in the data, not by schedule.

source: Langley (1977) BACON: A production system that discovers empirical laws (IJCAI-77)
finding: BACON is placed in a line of earlier programs (DENDRAL, meta-DENDRAL, MYCIN, AM) that reached rules explaining data. Its difference: it also constructs new attributes from old ones and uses the regularities found to direct the next round of data gathering.
numbers: No quantitative results are given in the 1977 paper; it is a design description (two pages).
limits: Short paper: no tests of speed or success rate, no comparison to alternatives.
agent_relevance: Early evidence is a demonstration, not a measured success rate. Treat claims of 'general discoverer' as unproven at this stage.

source: Langley (1979) Rediscovering physics with BACON.3 (IJCAI-79)
finding: BACON.3 (about 86 OPS2 productions in 7 sets) rediscovered five laws with one shared heuristic set. Data sit at levels of description: lower levels are observed, higher levels are hypotheses; defined terms are treated like observables, so the same heuristics recurse. Slope and intercept of a linear relation become new terms; product or ratio is chosen by the numbers involved.
numbers: Laws: ideal gas, Kepler third law, Coulomb, Ohm, Galileo (pendulum and constant acceleration). Ideal-gas run built pV at level 1, pV/T at level 2, pV/nT at level 3. Rule sets: 22 productions check term equivalence by decomposing to primitives; 8 mark irrelevant variables; 3 collapse hypotheses with identical conditions; 10 gather data by a factorial design. Ohm's law took the most computation (productions fired, working memory, conflict set).
limits: Variables are supplied by the programmer. Noise handled only by redefining LISP equal to ignore small differences. Generality claim rests on five tasks. Authors note the one heuristic not reused is 'misleading' since irrelevant variables could be added to every task.
agent_relevance: Recursive reuse of the same few heuristics at every level, plus a rule to stop varying variables that proved irrelevant, is a concrete model for a subgoal library with a 'drop what does not matter' operator.

source: Langley (1979) Rediscovering physics with BACON.3 (IJCAI-79)
finding: Order of data collection changes cost but not result. Varying irrelevant variables (weight, angle for the pendulum) first found them irrelevant at once; varying them last reached identical laws but needed more computation. Ideal gas with n varied first gave a different path: V/n, then V/nT, then pV/nT.
numbers: Two runs per task reported; same final laws. Path differs in terms built.
limits: Only two orderings per task were tried. No counts of the extra computation given in the text.
agent_relevance: Cheap early probes of irrelevance save work. Final answers can be order-robust while the path is not: so compare answers across orderings, not paths.

source: Langley, Bradshaw, Simon (1981) BACON.5: The discovery of conservation laws (IJCAI-81)
finding: BACON.5 adds symmetry and analogy. After a relation is found for one object, it is reused to cut the data to examine for the next object. Same data-driven heuristics: note constancies and trends, define theoretical terms, postulate intrinsic properties. Rediscovered Snell's law, conservation of momentum, Black's specific heat law, Joule's formulation of conservation of energy.
numbers: Ideal gas example in the paper: with n=1 and T=300, V falls as p rises, pV is considered and found constant at 2496.0 (R = 8.32, so nRT = 2496). Earlier laws re-found too: Coulomb, Kepler third, Ohm.
quote: one of many ways in which historical discoveries could have occurred
limits: Authors say it is 'not intended as a detailed model of historical discoveries' and covers only the data-to-regularity step, not choosing data, inventing instruments, deriving consequences of theory. Hand-prepared tables.
agent_relevance: Transfer a found relation to the symmetric case instead of re-searching: an 'exploit symmetry' operator that shrinks the space.

source: Kramer, Langley et al. (2023) Automated Scientific Discovery: From Equation Discovery to Autonomous Discovery Systems
finding: Survey names BACON the first equation-discovery system from data. It rests on the view that discovery 'is essentially problem solving'. BACON.1 to .5 ran on the PRISM production system and relied on correlating pairs of variables with all else held fixed. New terms (ratios, products) come from production rules. Noise is handled by a tolerance parameter. Later systems (LAGRAMGE, SINDy) drop the hold-all-else-constant limit and learn ODEs; SINDy uses sparse linear regression over products of derivatives.
numbers: BACON derives Kepler's third law D^3/P^2 = k by a chain of constructed terms until a near-constant value appears. Zytkow coupled real electrochemistry to FAHRENHEIT and later a robot that rediscovered Galileo's inclined plane law with empirical error.
limits: Secondary description. Survey says the ceteris-paribus assumption is strong and often impossible to meet in real experiments.
agent_relevance: Gives the lineage from BACON to modern symbolic regression and names the gap: systems that run alone yet report in forms scientists can inspect and steer. Our operator log fits that gap.

source: Kramer, Langley et al. (2023) Automated Scientific Discovery: From Equation Discovery to Autonomous Discovery Systems
finding: Adam is credited as the first largely autonomous system to find new knowledge: it identified 6 genes encoding orphan enzymes in yeast. It had a Prolog knowledge base of yeast metabolism, formed hypotheses by abduction with bioinformatics databases, then a planner chose metabolites for the growth medium; runs lasted up to 5 days. Eve uses active learning with Gaussian-process regression to pick K compounds per round, balancing exploration and exploitation.
numbers: Adam: 6 orphan-enzyme genes. Eve: TNP-470, an anti-cancer compound, repurposed against Plasmodium vivax.
limits: Secondary summary; primary papers by King et al. were paywalled this session (see unopened lines).
agent_relevance: Both robots run the same loop: hypothesis from knowledge base, planned experiment, measured result, update. Same shape as our generate-test loop with a hard external check.

source: Langley (2024) Integrated systems for computational scientific discovery (AAAI-24)
finding: Langley frames discovery as heuristic search in several spaces (qualitative relations, equations, process models, causal models). Each needs search operators, evaluation heuristics, a stopping rule and a search organisation. Research has focused on single components with little attention to their coordination. Simon (1966) proposed automating discovery; first successes came in the 1970s (DENDRAL, BACON).
numbers: No new measurements. Describes FAHRENHEIT as testing its induced laws with further experiments. Names eight component abilities that an integrated system needs.
limits: Position paper. Names on-line revision of accepted models (caloric, phlogiston) as a main unsolved challenge, since most systems work in batch.
agent_relevance: Supports the operators-as-heuristics reading and the claim that integration across components is the missing part. Revision must be on-line from new evidence, as in guardrail G2.

source: Langley (2024) Integrated systems for computational scientific discovery (AAAI-24)
finding: KEKADA (Kulkarni and Simon 1990) used a knowledge-rich route: it devised experiments to test hypotheses and explain anomalies, and rediscovered a process model of the urea cycle, following Hans Krebs. Adam (King et al. 2009) designed auxotrophic growth studies with gene knockouts, ran them on a robot manipulator and revised its causal model of how genes affect phenotypes.
numbers: No counts given here.
limits: Secondary description only.
agent_relevance: The contrast: BACON is data-driven (no surprise handling); KEKADA reacts to surprise by setting a new goal. That reaction is the impasse-trigger idea in our schema.

source: Dzeroski, Langley, Todorovski (2007) Computational discovery of scientific knowledge
finding: Simon outlined discovery as problem-space search. In the late 1970s, AM (Lenat) rediscovered concepts and conjectures in number theory from basic concepts and combining heuristics, and BACON rediscovered numeric laws from physics and chemistry from data and regularity heuristics. Both used data-driven induction of descriptive laws, shown on historical cases.
numbers: No effect sizes. Called 'the first compelling evidence' that computational discovery was possible.
limits: Review. Both early systems were demonstrated only where the answer was known; the authors say they had many limitations.
agent_relevance: Rediscovery shows the heuristic set is sufficient for known cases, not that it finds anything new.

source: Udrescu and Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman: a physics-inspired method for symbolic regression
finding: Recursive symbolic regression that combines a neural-net fit with physics tricks: dimensional analysis, polynomial fit, brute-force search, and tests for translational symmetry, separability and compositionality that split a hard problem into easier ones.
numbers: 100 Feynman Lectures equations: AI Feynman solved 100/100, Eureqa (commercial genetic programming) 71/100. On a harder physics-based set, success rose from 15% to 90%. Paper opens with Kepler: about 4 years and about 40 failed attempts to fit Mars data.
quote: previous publicly available software cracks only 71
limits: Known physics, so open to memorisation by language models (see LLM-SRBench). Hyperparameters and symbol sets were tuned; a few equations needed a second or third symbol set (1 or 2 extra hours). Eureqa ran on 4 CPUs with 300 data points.
agent_relevance: A cheap structural test that splits a problem is worth more than more sampling; this is the modern form of BACON's term construction.

source: Udrescu and Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman: a physics-inspired method for symbolic regression
finding: Search is staged by cost: try the cheap modules first (dimensional analysis, polynomial fit), then brute force over symbols in order of increasing complexity, and only then split the problem. Brute force is limited because strings of length n over s symbols number s^n.
numbers: Brute force uses a fixed small symbol set (optional functions in Table I) and a tolerance (1e-5 in the hyperparameter table); alphabet size and tolerance are the budget knobs.
limits: For the noise runs the paper says thresholds were not optimised for each mystery.
agent_relevance: Answers the question of how pruning budgets were set: a fixed symbol alphabet, a complexity cap and an error tolerance, with cheap modules first. Copyable as a staged-cost ladder.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR: Scientific equation discovery via programming with large language models (ICLR 2025)
finding: LLM proposes equation skeletons as Python programs, an optimiser (BFGS or Adam) fits constants against data, and an experience buffer of best programs is fed back (multi-island evolutionary loop). Generate-and-test with the LLM as generator and data fit as test. Beats symbolic-regression baselines, especially out of domain.
numbers: Four tasks (two oscillators, E. coli growth, stress-strain). About 2.5K iterations versus 2M+ for baselines. Settings: 4 skeletons per prompt, temperature 0.8, 2 in-context examples from the buffer. E. coli OOD NMSE about 0.0037 for LLM-SR versus above 1 for other methods.
limits: Tasks built to avoid recitation, but LLM-SRBench shows memorisation matters on classic equations. Backbones GPT-3.5 and Mixtral. Table layout was garbled in text extraction, so only prose figures are recorded.
agent_relevance: Splitting structure (LLM) from constants (optimiser), with data fit as the test, beats asking the model for the whole answer. Supports G3 and G5: code scores candidates.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR: Scientific equation discovery via programming with large language models (ICLR 2025)
finding: Ablation on Oscillation 2 with GPT-3.5: each part matters. Removing the natural-language problem description (prior) hurt considerably; limiting to one-line expressions hurt less; removing the iterative refinement loop and removing the separate optimiser both hurt a lot.
numbers: Without iterative refinement: NMSE 1.01e-1 in-domain, 1.81e-1 OOD. Without skeleton plus optimiser (end-to-end numbers from the LLM): 3.78e-1 in-domain, 3.75e-1 OOD. numpy+BFGS slightly beat torch+Adam, which authors put down to LLM skill with numpy code.
limits: One problem, one backbone for the ablation.
agent_relevance: The feedback loop from real fit error is the biggest single part, so it should be kept even when the model is strong.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: A new benchmark for scientific equation discovery with large language models
finding: Benchmark of 239 problems: LSR-Transform (111 Feynman equations rewritten into less common forms) and LSR-Synth (128 synthetic problems: chemistry 36, biology 24, physics 43, material science 25). Built so recall cannot solve them. Best system solves under a third.
numbers: Best symbolic accuracy 31.5% on LSR-Transform (LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini) and 28.1% on LSR-Synth. Direct prompting without data: GPT-4o-mini 7.21% on LSR-Transform. LLM-SR with Llama-3.1-8B reached 30.63%. LaSR got 5 to 13% symbolic accuracy but 46 to 50% numeric precision (Acc0.1).
quote: the best-performing system so far achieves only 31.5% symbolic accuracy
limits: Symbolic accuracy is judged by an LLM (GPT-4o) against ground truth. Only 24 to 43 problems per domain.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G3: numeric fit can be high while the form is wrong.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: A new benchmark for scientific equation discovery with large language models
finding: Memorisation check: simple LLM sampling (Llama-3.1-8B) on 100 Feynman problems shows sharp drops in numeric error curves and much lower symbolic error than on LSR-Transform or LSR-Synth. Authors read this as recall, not gradual discovery. At the same equation complexity, symbolic and numeric accuracy are lower on LSR-Transform than on original Feynman problems.
numbers: Figure 1 and Figure 4 of the paper; averages over all method-LLM pairs.
limits: The figure is read from curves; no single p-value or N beyond 100 Feynman problems.
agent_relevance: Any test of our agent on famous laws or puzzles is contaminated; use transformed or fresh variants.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: Towards data-driven discovery with large language models
finding: Benchmark of 264 real tasks from published papers (6 domains) and 903 synthetic tasks. Each task: dataset, metadata, goal in words; scored on context, variables and relationship match. Agents tested: CodeGen, ReAct, DataVoyager (planner with self-critic), Reflexion with oracle feedback, NoDataGuess.
numbers: Best system scores only 25%. ReAct and DataVoyager did not beat plain CodeGen; Reflexion with the oracle score as feedback (max 3 trials) improved significantly. Workflow: correlation analysis 55%, data selection 18%, summary statistics 18%; spatial analysis, pollen dating, ecological modelling 0%. Domain: biology 0%, engineering 7%, economics 25%, sociology 23%. Replication from papers took up to 90 person-hours per dataset.
limits: A domain-knowledge hint result reads 9.9% 'with' versus 17.5% 'without', which looks reversed; read as a gain from hints, unverified. About 30% of source analyses did not replicate cleanly in the authors' data work.
agent_relevance: Added reasoning prompts did not beat plain code; only a real external score signal helped. Matches G1/G2: improve from checked output, not self-critique.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards fully automated open-ended scientific discovery
finding: Pipeline that brainstorms ideas, edits code from a template, runs experiments, writes a paper and reviews it with an automated reviewer, with no human in the loop.
numbers: Under $15 per paper. Automated reviewer (GPT-4o, 5 reflection rounds, 5 ensembled reviews, 1-shot example) reached 70% accuracy on 500 ICLR 2022 papers versus 73% for human reviewers (NeurIPS 2021 consistency study); F1 0.57 versus 0.49; AUC 0.65 for both at a score threshold of 6.
limits: Reviewer cannot ask questions. Templates limit the domain (ML).
agent_relevance: Cheap end-to-end loop, but quality depends on the reviewer, which is itself a model.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards fully automated open-ended scientific discovery
finding: Failure list from the authors: hallucinated results (an early prompt demanding ablation tables made it invent one), invented facts such as the hardware, miscomparing the size of two numbers, failing to account for a metric change when comparing to baseline, poor citations, a hallucinated plot in a generated paper.
numbers: Fixes: instruct to include only results directly observed; store copies of all executed files for reproducibility.
quote: we do not recommend taking the scientific content of this version of The AI Scientist at face value
limits: Described qualitatively; no failure rates given.
agent_relevance: A direct checklist for guardrails: report only observed results, re-check comparisons after any metric change.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: Multi-agent generate, debate, evolve system: hypotheses are generated, reviewed for correctness, quality and novelty, ranked by Elo tournaments, and evolved. Quality by its own Elo metric rises with more compute.
numbers: Elo tracked over 203 research goals. On 15 expert-curated hard goals it eventually beat Gemini 2.0 Pro and Flash Thinking, o1, o3-mini-high, DeepSeek R1 and the expert best guess. Average expert preference rank 2.36 (of 4). Candidates for acute myeloid leukaemia were checked in vitro.
limits: Elo is auto-evaluated by the system's own judge, so the rise is partly self-grading. Only 15 curated goals. Few wet-lab checks.
agent_relevance: Tournament ranking by a model judge is what G5 warns about; the independent evidence is the wet-lab validation only.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber, Goodman (2024) Hypothesis search: Inductive reasoning with language models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Model proposes many hypotheses in words, they are filtered or summarised, each is turned into Python, run on the examples, and execution feedback refines it. A modern form of heuristic hypothesis generation plus test.
numbers: 100 random ARC tasks, GPT-4: direct 17%, programs only 23%, summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected hypotheses 33%, human-written hypotheses 45% (table); Icecuber non-LLM search 43%. GPT-4 held a correct hypothesis for only 49 tasks; of the 30 solved with summaries, 28 had a correct hypothesis before summarising. Human-selected hypotheses gave correct programs for 33 of 49 (67%). SyGuS 94.3% with 8 programs.
limits: One model, one 100-task sample, so a few points are noise. Human selection is not automatable. Text and table disagree on the human-written figure.
agent_relevance: The bottleneck is picking the right hypothesis, not coding it. Supports abstract first, concrete second, execution as the test.

source: Williams, Bilsland, Sparkes, ... King (2015) Cheaper faster drug development validated by the repositioning of drugs against neglected tropical diseases
finding: Robot Scientist Eve automates library screening, hit confirmation and lead generation through cycles of QSAR learning (Gaussian-process regression with active learning) and testing. An econometric model finds AI-selected screening cheaper than brute-force screening.
numbers: Maybridge Hitfinder library of about 14,400 compounds screened. Simulation: cost-optimal to screen between a third and a half of Eve's small library, in 96-compound loops.
limits: The saving is a simulation on one screen, not a controlled head-to-head.
agent_relevance: Choose what to test by predicted payoff; stop when the model says the rest is not worth testing.

source: Williams, Bilsland, Sparkes, ... King (2015) Cheaper faster drug development validated by the repositioning of drugs against neglected tropical diseases
finding: A validated discovery: the anti-cancer compound TNP-470 inhibits Plasmodium vivax DHFR.
numbers: IC50 0.16 micromolar for the parasite enzyme versus more than 165 micromolar for human DHFR, about 1000-fold selectivity. Confirmed in enzyme inhibition assays after Eve's yeast assay flagged it.
limits: Enzyme assay only, not a patient outcome.
agent_relevance: The hit came from a generate-test loop but was confirmed by an independent assay, which fits G3.

source: Chalmers/Eve group, with King (2026) Investigating uncharacterised genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae using robot scientists
finding: Eve tests a hypothesis about an uncharacterised yeast gene (YGR067C, proposed to regulate respiration at the diauxic shift). Predictions come from curated pathways and the Yeast9 genome-scale model and are tested on growth, transcript and metabolite data from the deletion strain.
numbers: About 880 of about 6,000 yeast ORFs remain uncharacterised. Deletion led to downregulation of some respiratory transcripts in the glucose phase; NAD+, NADP+ and NADH accumulated in the ethanol phase.
limits: One gene only; effects are described as suggestive. Author names not recorded.
agent_relevance: The robot-scientist pipeline still works in 2026, at the pace of one chosen hypothesis, not mass discovery.

source: King et al. (2009) The automation of science (Science)
finding: Adam: formed hypotheses by abduction, planned yeast growth experiments with knockouts, ran them on a robot, revised.
numbers: Not read; paywalled. Only the figure '6 orphan-enzyme genes' is available from a secondary source.
limits: Unopened. Do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Fetch before use.

source: King et al. (2004) Functional genomic hypothesis generation and experimentation by a robot scientist (Nature)
finding: Earlier robot scientist paper on yeast gene function, with active choice of experiments to cut cost.
numbers: Not read; page redirected to a login.
limits: Unopened. No numbers.
agent_relevance: Fetch before use.

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (Cognitive Science)
finding: KEKADA modelled the Krebs urea-cycle discovery with heuristics that choose the next experiment, notice surprises and set goals to explain them.
numbers: Not read; publisher blocked access. Only secondary description in Langley 2024.
limits: Unopened primary; heuristic list and experiment counts not recorded.
agent_relevance: Most relevant founding model for choosing experiments after surprise. Fetch next.

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific discovery: Computational explorations of the creative processes (MIT Press)
finding: Book collecting BACON.1 to .6, GLAUBER, STAHL, DALTON and others; argues discovery is ordinary problem solving by heuristic search.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Unopened.
agent_relevance: Source of the full heuristic list; cite via the opened papers until checked.
